questions.question: Explain the Hall effect. A current-carrying conductor is placed in a magnetic field perpendicular to the current. Describe qualitatively what happens and what the Hall voltage measures.
questions.answer:
When a current $I$ flows through a conductor in a transverse magnetic field $B$:

1. The magnetic (Lorentz) force deflects the charge carriers sideways: $F = qv_d B$ (where $v_d$ is drift velocity)
2. Charges accumulate on one side of the conductor, creating a transverse electric field $E_H$
3. Equilibrium: $qE_H = qv_d B \Rightarrow E_H = v_d B$
4. The **Hall voltage** $V_H = E_H \cdot w = v_d B w$ (where $w$ is the conductor width)

The Hall voltage measures:
- The **sign** of charge carriers (electrons vs. holes flip the sign of $V_H$)
- The **carrier density** $n$ via $V_H = \dfrac{IB}{nqt}$ (where $t$ is conductor thickness)

questions.question: A Hall probe (conductor width $w = 2\ \mathrm{mm}$, thickness $t = 0.5\ \mathrm{mm}$) carries current $I = 100\ \mathrm{mA}$ in a magnetic field $B = 0.5\ \mathrm{T}$ perpendicular to the current. The charge carriers are electrons ($n = 8\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$). Find: (a) the drift velocity, (b) the Hall voltage.
questions.answer:
**(a)** $I = nqv_d A$ where $A = wt$:

$v_d = \dfrac{I}{nqwt} = \dfrac{0.1}{8\times10^{28} \times 1.6\times10^{-19} \times 2\times10^{-3} \times 0.5\times10^{-3}}$

$= \dfrac{0.1}{8\times10^{28} \times 1.6\times10^{-25}} = \dfrac{0.1}{1.28\times10^4} \approx 7.81\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m/s}$

**(b)** $V_H = v_d B w = 7.81\times10^{-6} \times 0.5 \times 2\times10^{-3} = 7.81\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{V}$

Or using $V_H = IB/(nqt)$:

$V_H = \dfrac{0.1 \times 0.5}{8\times10^{28} \times 1.6\times10^{-19} \times 0.5\times10^{-3}} = \dfrac{0.05}{6.4\times10^6} \approx 7.81\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{V}$

questions.question: Derive the Hall voltage formula $V_H = \dfrac{IB}{nqt}$, where $I$ is the current, $B$ is the magnetic field, $n$ is the carrier density, $q$ is the carrier charge, and $t$ is the conductor thickness.
questions.answer:
At equilibrium, electric force balances magnetic force on each carrier:

$qE_H = qv_d B \Rightarrow E_H = v_d B$

Hall voltage: $V_H = E_H \cdot w = v_d B w$ (across width $w$)

Current: $I = nqv_d A = nqv_d(wt)$, so $v_d = \dfrac{I}{nqwt}$

Substitute:

$V_H = \dfrac{I}{nqwt} \cdot B \cdot w$

$$V_H = \dfrac{IB}{nqt}$$ ✓

Note: width $w$ cancels — the Hall voltage is independent of the conductor width.

questions.question: A Hall probe measures $V_H = 2\ \mathrm{mV}$ when carrying $I = 50\ \mathrm{mA}$ through a magnetic field $B = 0.8\ \mathrm{T}$. The probe thickness is $t = 1\ \mathrm{mm}$. Find the carrier density $n$.

In the Hall effect, a conductor of width $w = 5\ \mathrm{mm}$ carries current in the $+x$ direction. The magnetic field is in the $+z$ direction. In which direction does the Hall electric field point for: (a) positive charge carriers, (b) negative charge carriers (electrons)?
questions.answer:
Drift velocity in $+x$ direction.

**(a) Positive carriers:** $\vec{F} = q\vec{v}_d \times \vec{B} = q(\hat{x}) \times (\hat{z}) = q(-\hat{y})$

Positive carriers are pushed in $-y$ direction. They accumulate on the $-y$ side, creating $E_H$ in $+y$ direction (from $+$ to $-$... wait: high potential is on $-y$ side where positive charges accumulate).

$E_H$ points from $-y$ accumulation to $+y$ side? No: positive charges on $-y$ side $\Rightarrow$ higher potential on $-y$ side $\Rightarrow$ $E_H$ points in $+y$ direction (from high to low potential? — $E$ points from $+$ to $-$... $E$ points from $-y$ to $+y$, i.e., $+\hat{y}$). Hall voltage: bottom ($-y$) is positive.

**(b) Electrons:** Drift is still in $+x$ (conventional current $+x$), but $q < 0$:

$\vec{F} = (-e)(\hat{x}) \times (\hat{z}) = (-e)(-\hat{y}) = e\hat{y}$

Electrons pushed in $+y$ direction. Negative charges accumulate on $+y$ side $\Rightarrow$ $E_H$ points in $+y$ direction (away from $-y$ toward $+y$... actually $E$ points from where positive is to where negative is, i.e., from $-y$ side (now deficient in electrons, so positive) toward $+y$ side (excess electrons, negative)): $E_H$ in $-y$ direction.

Conclusion: **Hall voltage sign reverses** between positive and negative carriers — this is how the Hall effect identifies carrier type.

questions.question: A semiconductor Hall bar carries $I = 10\ \mathrm{mA}$ in a field $B = 0.3\ \mathrm{T}$. The measured Hall voltage is $V_H = 15\ \mathrm{mV}$, with the positive terminal on the right side (when current is in $+x$ and $B$ is in $+z$). The thickness is $t = 0.5\ \mathrm{mm}$. Find $n$ and identify the carrier type.
questions.answer:
$n = \dfrac{IB}{qV_H t} = \dfrac{10\times10^{-3} \times 0.3}{1.6\times10^{-19} \times 15\times10^{-3} \times 0.5\times10^{-3}}$

$= \dfrac{3\times10^{-3}}{1.2\times10^{-24}} = 2.5\times10^{21}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$

For $+x$ current and $+z$ field, positive carriers would accumulate on the right (in $-y$ direction). The positive Hall terminal on the right suggests **positive holes** are the majority carriers — this is a **p-type semiconductor**.

questions.question: A metal strip (electron conductor) of thickness $t = 0.1\ \mathrm{mm}$ and width $w = 10\ \mathrm{mm}$ carries $I = 5\ \mathrm{A}$ in a magnetic field $B = 2\ \mathrm{T}$. Carrier density $n = 5\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$. Find $V_H$.
questions.answer:
$V_H = \dfrac{IB}{nqt} = \dfrac{5 \times 2}{5\times10^{28} \times 1.6\times10^{-19} \times 0.1\times10^{-3}}$

$= \dfrac{10}{5\times10^{28} \times 1.6\times10^{-23}} = \dfrac{10}{8\times10^5} = 1.25\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{V} = 12.5\ \mu\mathrm{V}$

Hall voltages in metals are very small due to the high carrier density.

questions.question: Explain why Hall voltages are much larger in semiconductors than in metals, even for the same current and field.
questions.answer:
$V_H = \dfrac{IB}{nqt}$

The Hall voltage is **inversely proportional to carrier density $n$**.

- Metals: $n \sim 10^{28}$–$10^{29}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ (very high — one free electron per atom)
- Semiconductors: $n \sim 10^{16}$–$10^{22}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ (much lower — only thermally excited or doped carriers)

For the same $I$, $B$, $t$: a semiconductor with $n = 10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ gives a Hall voltage roughly $10^8$–$10^9$ times larger than a metal with $n = 10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$.

This is why Hall sensors are made of semiconducting materials (Si, GaAs, InSb) — the signals are large enough to measure practically.

questions.question: A Hall sensor is used to measure an unknown magnetic field $B$. The sensor has $n = 2\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $t = 0.2\ \mathrm{mm}$, carries $I = 20\ \mathrm{mA}$, and reads $V_H = 1.0\ \mathrm{V}$. Find $B$.
questions.answer:
$V_H = \dfrac{IB}{nqt} \Rightarrow B = \dfrac{V_H nqt}{I}$

$B = \dfrac{1.0 \times 2\times10^{22} \times 1.6\times10^{-19} \times 0.2\times10^{-3}}{0.02}$

$= \dfrac{1.0 \times 2\times10^{22} \times 3.2\times10^{-23}}{0.02}$

$= \dfrac{1.0 \times 0.64}{0.02} = \dfrac{0.64}{0.02} = 32\ \mathrm{T}$

(Very strong field — this would be in a research magnet.)

questions.question: Show that the Hall coefficient $R_H = 1/(nq)$ is a material constant, and find its value for copper ($n = 8.5\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $q = -e = -1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$).
questions.answer:
From $V_H = \dfrac{IB}{nqt}$, define the Hall coefficient $R_H$ such that:

$V_H = R_H \dfrac{IB}{t}$

Comparing: $R_H = \dfrac{1}{nq}$

This depends only on the carrier density and charge — a material constant.

For copper (electrons, $q = -e$):

$R_H = \dfrac{1}{nq} = \dfrac{1}{8.5\times10^{28} \times (-1.6\times10^{-19})} = \dfrac{1}{-1.36\times10^{10}}$

$R_H = -7.35\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m^3/C}$

Negative sign confirms electrons are the carriers. Measuring $R_H$ experimentally gives $n$ and the sign of carriers.
